f0-t6.title: The learning loop: predict, measure the loss, adjust, repeat

frames.caption: Three houses. Size is the feature; price is the label — the right answer the model has to learn to predict.
1 · Predict. The model is ŷ = w·size + b. It starts knowing nothing (w = 0), so it predicts £0 for every house.
2 · Loss: how wrong is it? Each red gap is one error. Square the gaps and take the average: loss = 69,900.
3 · Adjust. The gradient says "tilt the line up". One step moves w to 4.66: too far. Now the model guesses too high.
Loop again: predict, measure, adjust. w = 2.08 is now too low, but the loss has already fallen to 6,561.
w = 3.51. Each swing overshoots by less than the one before.
w = 3.05, loss 18. Closing in.
After 1,000 loops: w ≈ 3.00 and the loss is almost 0. The model has learned that each m² adds about £3,000.
Now test it on a house it has never seen: 100 m² → about £300k. If it does well on new data, deploy it.
Three houses. Size is the feature; price is the label — the right answer the model has to learn to predict.
1 · Predict. The model is ŷ = w·size + b. It starts knowing nothing (w = 0), so it predicts £0 for every house.
2 · Loss: how wrong is it? Each red gap is one error. Square the gaps and take the average: loss = 69,900.
Same loop, learning rate 10 times bigger (0.001). One step sends w to 46.6: a near-vertical line. Loss: 14.8 million.
The next step overshoots the other way, even further: w = −630.7. The line points straight down, off the chart. Loss: 3.1 billion.
Three steps later w is 1.9 million and the loss is about 3 × 10¹⁶. Every step lands further from the answer than the last. Too big a step never settles: make it smaller.

f0-t1.title: One grid of numbers, many ways to look at it

frames.caption: np.arange(12) makes the numbers 0 to 11 in one row. One direction, 12 long: shape (12,).
reshape(3, 4) folds the same 12 numbers into 3 rows of 4. Nothing is copied or changed; only the shape is new: (3, 4).
A[1, 2] means row 1, column 2. Counting starts at 0, so that is the second row and third column: 6.
A[:, 0]: the colon means "every row". So this is column 0 of every row: [0, 4, 8], shape (3,).
A[1] with one index picks a whole row: [4, 5, 6, 7]. Missing indexes mean "all of that direction".
A[A > 6] keeps only the cells where the test is True. This is a boolean mask, and the result is always flat.
A.T (transpose) swaps rows and columns: the 3 × 4 grid becomes 4 × 3. Row 0 [0, 1, 2, 3] is now column 0.

f0-t2.title: Broadcasting: stretching size-1 directions so shapes fit

frames.caption: scores is one column, shape (3, 1). bonus is one row, shape (1, 3). We want every score plus every bonus.
NumPy lines the shapes up from the right and compares each pair. Two sizes fit if they are equal, or if one of them is 1.
A size of 1 stretches to match. scores is stretched across into 3 columns. No memory is copied: NumPy just re-reads the same column.
bonus is stretched down into 3 rows. Now both are (3, 3).
Add cell by cell. Nine additions, one line of code, no Python loop: that is vectorisation.
Each cell is one score plus one bonus. Bottom right: 90 + 10 = 100.
You meant to add two lists of 3 numbers pairwise: [1, 2, 3] + [10, 20, 30] → [11, 22, 33]. But b is a column, shape (3, 1).
A 1-D array of shape (3,) lines up with the last direction, so it acts like a row, (1, 3). Row + column: both stretch.
No error, but you get 9 numbers instead of 3. Every later step can now be silently wrong.
Fix: make the shapes match on purpose (b.ravel() gives shape (3,)). Then assert the shape you expect, so a test catches it.

f0-t3.title: Reading loss curves: what healthy and broken training look like

frames.caption: Plot the loss after every training step. Step on the x-axis, loss on the y-axis.
Early on, the loss drops fast: the model picks up the easy patterns first.
Then the curve bends and flattens. Each step still helps, but only a little.
A healthy loss curve: a fast fall, then a slow, steady level. If it is still sloping down at the end, train for longer.
Now plot two curves: loss on the training data (blue) and on held-out validation data (pink).
At first both fall together: the model is learning patterns that work on new data too.
Then they split. Training loss keeps falling while validation loss climbs: the model is memorising the training set. That is overfitting.
Keep the model from the lowest point of the validation curve. Stopping there is called early stopping.
With the learning rate set too high, each step jumps over the bottom of the valley.
The loss bounces up and down instead of falling. Spikes like these are the warning sign.
Often it climbs and finally turns into NaN ("not a number"). The fix: divide the learning rate by 3 to 10 and try again.
This loss falls from 1,000 to 0.01. On a normal y-axis, everything after step 20 looks like zero, so the late progress is hidden.
The same numbers on a log scale: each gridline is 10 times smaller than the one above. The loss is still improving steadily all the way.
That is why loss curves are usually drawn with plt.yscale("log"): small changes late in training become visible.

f0-t4.title: Git: where your changes live, and how branches work

frames.caption: Your change starts in the working folder: the files you edit. Git sees that model.py changed, but has saved nothing yet.
git add puts the change in the staging area: "this is going into my next snapshot". You choose exactly what to include.
git commit saves a snapshot in your local repository, with a message saying why. You can always come back to it.
git push copies your commits to GitHub: an online backup, and proof of your work that employers can see.
Each dot is a commit: a snapshot of the whole project, plus a message. HEAD marks where you are.
Commits form a line, newest on the right. Each one points back to the one before, so the history is never lost.
git switch -c experiment starts a new branch here. A branch is only a label on a commit, so this is instant and free.
Commit on the branch. main has not changed at all, so a risky idea can never break your working code.
Meanwhile main moves on too: a typo fix. The two lines of work now differ.
git merge experiment joins them in a merge commit. If both sides changed the same line, Git stops and you choose by hand: a merge conflict.

f0-t5.title: Why tests on decimals need a tolerance, and how a test catches a bug

frames.caption: Computers store decimals in binary, so most of them can only be stored approximately. 0.1 + 0.2 really comes out as 0.30000000000000004.

shapes.text: zoomed in: the whole line is 0.0000000000000002 wide

frames.caption: == asks "exactly the same?" The two numbers differ in the 17th decimal place, so the answer is False.

shapes.text: zoomed in: the whole line is 0.0000000000000002 wide

frames.caption: np.allclose asks "close enough?" It allows a tiny gap (about 0.000003 near 0.3). This gap is far smaller, so the answer is True.

shapes.text: allowed gap: the whole line, and far beyond
zoomed in: the whole line is 0.0000000000000002 wide

frames.caption: A test runs your code on a case where you already know the right answer. Here: softmax of [1000, 1001, 1002] must give probabilities that sum to 1.
Softmax starts with exp(x). But exp(1000) is far bigger than the largest number a float can hold, so it overflows to inf.
Dividing inf by inf gives NaN. The test fails, and you found the bug before it reached real training.
The fix: subtract the largest value first. [1000, 1001, 1002] becomes [−2, −1, 0]. The answer is mathematically the same, and nothing overflows.
Divide by the sum (1.503): [0.090, 0.245, 0.665]. They sum to 1, so the test passes. Keep the test, and the bug can never come back.

f1-t1.title: Building every point from two arrows

frames.caption: Two arrows: [1, 0] in green and [0, 1] in pink. A vector is an arrow from the origin, and also simply a list of numbers.
Scale: 3·[1, 0] = [3, 0]. Multiplying by a number stretches the arrow; a negative number would flip it round.
Add tip to tail: 3·[1, 0] + 2·[0, 1] = [3, 2]. Scaling some vectors and adding them up is called a linear combination.
Try every pair of weights and the dots fill the whole plane. The span of [1, 0] and [0, 1] is everything, so these two arrows form a basis.
Now [1, 2] and [2, 4]. The second is just 2 × the first, so every combination lands on one line. Their span is a line: they are dependent, and not a basis.

f1-t2.title: A matrix moves the whole grid at once

frames.caption: Before: the ordinary grid. Green î = [1, 0], pink ĵ = [0, 1], and a yellow vector [1, 1].
Apply A. î lands on [2, 0] and ĵ on [0, 1.5]: exactly the two columns of A. Grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced.
[1, 1] is 1·î + 1·ĵ, so it lands on 1·[2, 0] + 1·[0, 1.5] = [2, 1.5]. Know where the columns go, and you know where everything goes.
A shear: [[1, 1], [0, 1]]. Start from the ordinary grid.
î stays at [1, 0]; ĵ tips over to [1, 1]. Every square leans into a parallelogram, but lines stay straight and the origin stays put.
A yellow unit square. R rotates by 90°; S shears (pushes the top sideways). Does the order matter?
First R: the square turns a quarter-turn anticlockwise.
Then S shears it. This combined move is the product S·R (read right to left).
Now the other order. Back to the start…
First S: the square leans over.
Then R turns it. R·S lands in a different place from S·R, so for matrices AB ≠ BA: the order matters.

f1-t3.title: The determinant: how much area grows, and whether space flips

frames.caption: The unit square has area 1. The determinant of a matrix is the area this square has after the matrix moves it.
[[2, 0], [0, 1.5]] stretches x by 2 and y by 1.5. The square becomes a 2 × 1.5 rectangle: det = 3, so every area triples.
A shear [[1, 1], [0, 1]] leans the square over. Same base, same height, so the area is still 1: det = 1·1 − 1·0 = 1.
[[0, 1], [1, 0]] swaps x and y. The area is still 1, but î and ĵ have changed places: space is flipped like a mirror image. det = −1.
[[1, 2], [0.5, 1]]: both columns lie on the same line, so the square is squashed flat. Area 0, det = 1·1 − 2·0.5 = 0. This matrix can't be undone.

f1-t4.title: Solving Ax = b, and why a squashing matrix has no undo

frames.caption: Solve 2x + y = 3 and x + 3y = 5. As a matrix: which vector does A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]] move onto b = [3, 5]?
Apply A to the whole grid. The vector x = [0.8, 1.4] lands exactly on b. So x = [0.8, 1.4] is the solution.
The inverse A⁻¹ undoes A: it moves the grid back and carries b back to x. That is x = A⁻¹b. In code, np.linalg.solve(A, b) does this.
Now A = [[1, 2], [2, 4]]. Its second column is 2 × the first. Watch two different vectors: [1, 1] and [3, 0].
Apply A: the whole plane is squashed onto one line. Both vectors land on the same point, [3, 6].
Given only [3, 6], you can't tell which vector it came from, so there is no inverse. And b = [3, 5] is off the line: no x reaches it at all.

f1-t5.title: The dot product is the length of a shadow

frames.caption: a = [3, 4] and b = [1, 0]. Multiply matching entries and add: 3·1 + 4·0 = 3. Now see what that number means.
Shine a light straight down onto b's line. The shadow of a is its projection, [3, 0]. Because b has length 1, the shadow's length is the dot product: 3.
Turn a closer to b (still length 5) and the shadow grows: a = [4, 3], a·b = 4. The more two vectors point the same way, the bigger the dot product.
At 90° the shadow disappears: a·b = 0. The vectors are orthogonal (at right angles).
Past 90° the shadow points backwards: a·b = −3. A negative dot product means the vectors point away from each other.

f1-t6.title: Eigenvectors: the directions a matrix only stretches

frames.caption: Eight arrows, each on its own dashed line. Watch which ones leave their line when A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] moves the plane.
Most arrows are knocked off their line: [1, 0] turns into [2, 1]. But two directions stay exactly on their dashed lines.
Along [1, 1] each arrow is simply stretched 3 times: an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ = 3. Along [1, −1] arrows don't change at all: λ = 1.
So A is simple in disguise: stretch 3× along [1, 1] and leave [1, −1] alone. Apply it 10 times and the [1, 1] part grows by 3¹⁰ while the rest stays put.

f1-t7.title: PCA: find the direction where the data spreads most

frames.caption: 40 data points with 2 features. The cloud is stretched along one diagonal direction, and it sits away from the origin.
Step 1: centre it. Subtract the mean of each feature, so the cloud sits around the origin.
Try a direction and drop every point onto it (pink shadows). Along this one the shadows bunch up: variance only 0.35.
The first principal direction is the one where the shadows spread out most: variance 6.12. It keeps 97% of all the variance.
The second direction is at right angles to the first and holds the remaining 3%. SVD finds both at once, ordered by spread.
Keep PC1 only: every point moves onto the yellow line. Two numbers per point become one, and little information is lost.

f1-t8.title: The derivative is a slope; the chain rule multiplies rates

frames.caption: f(x) = x². How fast is it changing at x = 1?
Nudge x by h = 1.2 and draw the line through both points. Its slope, (4.84 − 1) / 1.2, is 3.2.
A smaller nudge, h = 0.6: the slope is 2.6.
h = 0.2: slope 2.2. As the nudge shrinks, the slope settles on one number…
…the derivative, f′(1) = 2 × 1 = 2: the slope of the tangent line that just touches the curve.
At x = −1.5 the slope is −3: the curve is going downhill there. The derivative changes from point to point.
At x = 0 the slope is 0: flat. The bottom of a valley is always flat, which is how we find minimums.
A function inside a function: u = 3x + 1, then f = u². At x = 1: u = 4 and f = 16.
Nudge x by 0.01, to 1.01…
…u moves 3 times as much: 4 → 4.03. The inner rate is du/dx = 3.
…and f moves 2u = 8 times as much as u: 16 → 16.24. The outer rate is df/du = 2u = 8.
Multiply the rates along the chain: df/dx = 8 × 3 = 24. That is the chain rule. Backpropagation is exactly this, repeated through every layer of a network.
A bowl seen from above: f(x, y) = x² + 2y². Each ring is a contour, joining points of equal height. You stand at (1.5, 1), height 4.25.
Step east and hold y still: the height rises at ∂f/∂x = 2x = 3 per unit step.
Step north and hold x still: it rises at ∂f/∂y = 4y = 4 per unit step.
Put them together: the gradient [3, 4]. It points straight uphill, at right angles to the ring, and its length √(3² + 4²) = 5 is the steepness.
Gradient descent steps the other way, −∇f. With learning rate 0.1 you land at (1.2, 0.6), where the height is only 2.16.
Repeat, and the steps walk down into the bowl, each one at right angles to the ring it starts from, until the gradient is zero at the bottom.

f1-t10.title: Gradient descent: the step size decides everything

frames.caption: f(w) = w², starting at w = 4. The slope there is 2w = 8, so downhill is to the left.
One step: w ← w − 0.1 × 8 = 3.2.
w = 2.56. The slope is gentler here, so the step is shorter, all by itself.
w = 2.048. Each step multiplies w by 1 − 2 × 0.1 = 0.8.
w = 0.839, gliding smoothly to the bottom. After 50 steps it would be about 0.00006.
Same start, learning rate 0.01: ten times smaller steps.
w = 3.92. Each step only multiplies w by 0.98.
w = 3.842. Each step only multiplies w by 0.98.
w = 3.765. Each step only multiplies w by 0.98.
w = 3.689. Each step only multiplies w by 0.98.
w = 3.616. Each step only multiplies w by 0.98.
w = 3.543: barely moved. It will get there, but it needs hundreds of steps.
Learning rate 0.9. Now each step multiplies w by 1 − 1.8 = −0.8.
w = -3.2: it jumps across the valley every step, but lands a little lower each time.
w = 2.56: it jumps across the valley every step, but lands a little lower each time.
w = -2.048: it jumps across the valley every step, but lands a little lower each time.
w = 1.638: it jumps across the valley every step, but lands a little lower each time.
w = -1.311: it jumps across the valley every step, but lands a little lower each time.
w = 1.049. It does converge, but it wastes steps bouncing from side to side.
Learning rate 1.1: each step multiplies w by 1 − 2.2 = −1.2.
w = -4.8: it overshoots to the other side and lands higher than before.
w = 5.76: it overshoots to the other side and lands higher than before.
w = -6.91: it overshoots to the other side and lands higher than before.
w = 8.29: off the chart. Every step makes it worse; the loss explodes to infinity, then NaN.

f1-t11.title: A distribution is what many random draws settle into

frames.caption: Roll a fair die 6 times. The bars are lumpy and the average is 3.83: with so few rolls, chance dominates.
60 rolls: closer to even, average 3.2.
600 rolls: every bar is near the dashed line at 1/6, and the average is 3.45.
6,000 rolls: the bars match the distribution (1/6 each), and the average, 3.49, has settled near the expectation of 3.5. You can never roll 3.5; it is the long-run average.
Draw 50 values from a Gaussian (normal) distribution. The histogram is rough.
500 values: a hump appears, centred on the mean μ.
5,000 values: the histogram traces the bell-shaped density curve (yellow). For continuous values, probability is the area under this curve.
About 68% of values fall within one standard deviation σ of the mean, and about 95% within two. σ measures the spread.
1,000 people. Each dot stands for 10 of them.
1% are sick: 10 people, the one red dot. The other 990 are healthy.
Test everyone. It catches 99% of the sick (9.9 people) but also raises a false alarm for 5% of the healthy: 49.5 people, about 5 dots.
Now look only at the people who tested positive: about 59 of them. Only 9.9 are actually sick.
So P(sick | positive) = 9.9 / 59.4 ≈ 17%. The test is good, but the disease is rare, and false alarms from the many healthy people swamp the true cases.
Same test, but now 5% of people are sick: 50 people, 5 red dots.
Positives: 49.5 of the sick, plus 5% of 950 healthy = 47.5 false alarms.
Now P(sick | positive) = 49.5 / 97 ≈ 51%, three times higher. Same test, very different answer: the starting rate (the prior) matters enormously.

f1-t13.title: Maximum likelihood: pick what makes your data most probable

frames.caption: 10 coin flips: 7 heads and 3 tails. Which value of p, the chance of heads, explains this data best?
Try p = 0.3. The chance of exactly this sequence is p⁷(1 − p)³ = 0.00008: tiny. 7 heads would be surprising.
p = 0.9: 0.00048. Worse again: with p = 0.9 you would expect more than 7 heads.
Try every p and draw the likelihood curve. It peaks at p = 0.7, the fraction of heads you saw. That is the maximum likelihood estimate.
Eight measurements (orange dots). Model them as a Gaussian with spread 1 and an unknown mean μ. Try μ = 3: most dots sit far out in the tail, where the curve is low.
μ = 7: better for the right-hand dots, worse for the left. The likelihood multiplies the curve's height at every dot.
The best μ is 5.4, which is exactly the average of the data. For a Gaussian, maximum likelihood gives the sample mean, and maximising it is the same as minimising squared error.

f1-t14.title: How much can you trust one number from a sample?

frames.caption: A model's true accuracy is 85%, but in real life you never get to see that. You only see its score on a test set of 200 examples.
One test set: 89% correct. Standard error √(p(1 − p)/n) ≈ 2.5%, so the 95% interval is about ±5%: the green bar.
A different test set gives a different score and a different interval. Each one is a little off.
Twenty test sets: 18 of the 20 intervals catch the true value and 2 miss (red). That is what "95% confidence" means: the method catches the truth about 95% of the time.
Roll one die 3,000 times: a flat histogram. Every face is equally likely.
Now average 2 dice each time. Middle values become more common.
Average 5 dice: a hump around 3.5.
Average 20 dice: a narrow bell curve. That is the central limit theorem: averages are roughly Gaussian whatever you start from, and they get narrower as you average more.

f1-t15.title: Cross-entropy: the price of being wrong, and confidently wrong

frames.caption: The picture shows a dog. The model gives dog 0.7. Cross-entropy only looks at the probability of the true class: loss = −log 0.7 = 0.357.
Confident and right: dog 0.99. Loss −log 0.99 ≈ 0.01, almost nothing.
Unsure: one third each. Loss −log(1/3) ≈ 1.1.
Confident and wrong: dog only 0.05. Loss −log 0.05 ≈ 3.0. The curve shoots up near 0, so confident mistakes are punished hardest.
A coin that lands heads 70% of the time. You can guess a little better than chance, so the entropy is a bit under the 1-bit maximum: 0.88 bits.
Heads 99% of the time: hardly any surprise left, 0.08 bits.
Four equally likely outcomes: log₂ 4 = 2 bits, like two fair coin flips.
Eight equally likely outcomes: 3 bits. More equally likely options means more uncertainty.

f1-t16.title: Convex bowls have one bottom; constraints touch the rings

frames.caption: A convex bowl, f(w) = w². Drop three marbles at different places and let gradient descent roll them.
They all head the same way: down.
Closing in on the same bottom.
All three end at w = 0. In a convex function there is only one valley, so the start doesn't matter: any minimum you find is the best one.
A non-convex curve, w⁴ − 3w² + w, with two valleys. Same three kinds of start.
Each marble rolls into whichever valley it starts above.
They are splitting up.
Two end in the deep left valley (w ≈ −1.30) and one gets stuck in the shallow right one (w ≈ 1.13). Where you start decides where you finish.
Minimise x² + y² (rings around the origin), but only on the pink line x + y = 1. At (−0.6, 1.6) the value is 2.92.
Slide along the line: at (0, 1) the value is 1. The yellow arrow (the gradient of x² + y²) still points across the line at an angle, so we can do better.
At (0.5, 0.5) the ring just touches the line, and the yellow gradient lines up with the pink one (the line's own gradient). Nowhere lower on the line: value 0.5.
That is the Lagrange condition: ∇f = λ∇g. Solving 2x = λ, 2y = λ, x + y = 1 gives x = y = 0.5 and λ = 1.

f2-t1.title: Train, validation and test: three jobs for three slices of data

frames.caption: 20 rows of data, each with its features and its label. First, shuffle, so each slice is a fair mix.
Shuffled. Now cut it into three parts that never share a row.
Training set (70%): the model learns its weights from these rows only.
Validation set (15%): compare models and settings — learning rate, depth, k — and keep the best. The model never trains on it.
Test set (15%): locked away. Use it exactly once, at the very end, for the honest final score. Tuning on it would make that score a lie.

f2-t2.title: Least squares: the line with the smallest total squared error

frames.caption: Ten data points. We want the straight line ŷ = wx + b that sits as close as possible to all of them.
A flat guess, ŷ = 6.3. Each red line is an error. Least squares turns each error into a square and adds up their areas.
Tilting the line shrinks most of the squares.
The best line makes the total area of the squares as small as possible. The normal equation finds it in one step: ŷ = 0.62x + 3.15.
Gradient descent starts from w = 0, b = 0 and improves the line a little at a time.
After 4000 steps it has reached the same line the normal equation found in one go: ŷ = 0.62x + 3.15.

f2-t3.title: Logistic regression: squash a score into a probability

frames.caption: Did a student pass (1) or fail (0), given hours studied? We want P(pass) for any number of hours.
A straight line (linear regression) gives a score, but it runs below 0 and above 1. That can't be a probability.
The sigmoid σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) squashes the score z = wx + b into the range 0 to 1: an S-shaped curve, fitted by minimising cross-entropy.
Read off a probability: after 6.9 hours, P(pass) = 0.85. Far from the middle the curve flattens near 0 or 1: confident.
Predict "pass" when P > 0.5. That happens where z = 0, at 4.9 hours: the decision boundary. Points on the wrong side are the model's mistakes.

f2-t4.title: Penalising big weights: L2 shrinks, L1 switches off

frames.caption: Eight weights from an ordinary fit, with no penalty (λ = 0).
Add an L2 penalty, λ·Σw². Every weight shrinks by the same factor, 1 / (1 + λ).
Bigger λ, smaller weights. The big ones shrink the most in absolute terms, because the penalty grows with w².
Even at λ = 4, no weight reaches exactly 0. L2 makes everything small, but keeps every feature in play.
The same eight weights, no penalty.
Add an L1 penalty, λ·Σ|w|. Each weight is pulled towards 0 by the same fixed amount, so the smallest ones hit exactly 0: 2 already.
λ = 1.5: 4 weights are exactly 0. Those features have been switched off.
λ = 4: only 2 features survive. L1 gives sparse models, which also act as automatic feature selection.

f2-t5.title: Too simple, just right, too wiggly

frames.caption: 12 noisy points from a smooth curve (dashed). Fit polynomials of growing degree and compare.
Degree 1, a straight line: too simple to follow the curve. High bias — it misses on training data too (train error 0.27).
Degree 3: follows the real shape. Training error 0.05, validation error 0.06: both low.
Degree 9: bends to pass close to every training point (train error 0.031), but swings wildly in between. High variance: validation error 0.15.
Now fit every degree from 1 to 9 and plot both errors.
Training error (blue) only ever goes down: more flexibility always fits the training points better.
Validation error (pink) falls, then rises again. The bottom of that U, degree 5, is the sweet spot. To the left: underfitting (bias). To the right: overfitting (variance).

f2-t6.title: Precision, recall and the threshold that trades them

frames.caption: The model gives each transaction a fraud score. Grey dots are innocent, green are real fraud. Everything right of the yellow threshold gets flagged.
The confusion matrix counts the four outcomes. Precision: of what we flagged, how much was fraud? Recall: of all fraud, how much did we catch?
Lower the threshold: we catch more fraud (recall up) but flag more innocent people (precision down).
Raise it: fewer false alarms (precision up), but more fraud slips through (recall down). The right threshold depends on which mistake costs more.
Flag nothing: accuracy is still 75%, because most transactions are innocent. Yet recall is 0. Accuracy alone can hide a useless model.
Start with a very high threshold: nothing flagged, so both rates are 0 (bottom left).
Lower it step by step and plot true positive rate (recall) against false positive rate.
A good model climbs steeply: it catches fraud before it starts flagging many innocents.
The area under this curve (AUC) is 0.96: the chance a random fraud scores higher than a random innocent. 0.5 is guessing (the dashed line); 1.0 is perfect.

f2-t7.title: Cross-validation, and how test data leaks into training

frames.caption: Split the data into 5 equal folds. Round 1: train on folds 2–5, test on fold 1.
Round 2: a different fold is the test fold. Every row gets tested exactly once over the 5 rounds.
Round 3: a different fold is the test fold. Every row gets tested exactly once over the 5 rounds.
Round 4: a different fold is the test fold. Every row gets tested exactly once over the 5 rounds.
Round 5: a different fold is the test fold. Every row gets tested exactly once over the 5 rounds.
Average the five scores: 0.842 ± 0.021. The spread tells you how much one lucky or unlucky split could have misled you.
A common leak: scaling with the mean and standard deviation of ALL the data, test rows included. Information about the test set has crept into training.
The fix: compute the mean and standard deviation from the training rows only, then apply those same numbers to the test rows.

f2-t8.title: Scaling features, and turning categories into numbers

frames.caption: One feature is in thousands (size in m²·10), the other in single digits (rooms). The loss surface becomes a long, narrow valley.
Gradient descent zig-zags across the steep direction and crawls along the shallow one. One learning rate can't suit both.
Standardise each feature: (value − mean) / std. The valley becomes round.
Now the gradient points straight at the bottom, and the same number of steps gets much closer.
A category, like colour, is not a number. Coding red = 1, green = 2, blue = 3 invents an order and a distance: it says green sits between red and blue.
One-hot encoding gives each category its own column with a single 1. Every pair of colours is now equally far apart, and no order is invented.

f2-t9.title: k-nearest neighbours: let the closest examples vote

frames.caption: Two classes, A (blue) and B (pink). A new point (?) arrives. There is no training: we just look at the data.
k = 1: the single nearest point is a B, 1 away. Prediction: B.
k = 3: the three nearest are B, A, A. The majority says A. The answer depends on k.
k = 5: 4 A against 1 B, so A. Small k follows every bump in the data (high variance); large k smooths it out (high bias). Pick k with validation data.

f2-t10.title: A decision tree asks the question that makes the groups purest

frames.caption: 14 points, 6 blue (A) and 8 pink (B). Mixed together, Gini impurity is 0.49. A tree asks yes/no questions to make the groups purer.
Try every feature and threshold; keep the one that lowers impurity most. Best first question: x < 3? The right side is all B (Gini 0).
The left side is still mixed (Gini 0.44). Ask again, only there: y < 2.5? Now both parts are pure.
Done: every leaf is pure, and the tree reads as plain if-statements. The boundary is made of straight, axis-aligned cuts, so a diagonal boundary would need a staircase of many cuts.

shapes.text: if x<3 and y<2.5: A else: B

frames.caption: How does the tree choose x < 3? It tries every threshold. Here: 8 points labelled Y or N. Try x < 1.5 and measure the weighted Gini of the two sides.
Slide the threshold along. Each cut gets a score: the Gini of each side, weighted by how many points it holds.
After trying them all, the lowest score wins: x < 4.5. A tree repeats this search at every node, for every feature.

f2-t11.title: Many trees beat one: averaging (bagging) and correcting (boosting)

frames.caption: 26 noisy points. A single deep tree is jumpy: it follows the noise in whatever sample it was given.
Tree 1, trained on a bootstrap sample (rows drawn at random, with repeats): a jagged staircase.
Trees 2 and 3, on different random samples, make different mistakes.
Average 30 such trees (a random forest also picks random features). The mistakes cancel out and the average (green) is much smoother: lower variance, same low bias.
Boosting starts with a flat guess: the average. The red lines are what is still wrong (the residuals).
Fit one tiny tree (a single split, a "stump") to the residuals, and add a small step of it.
Each new stump fixes what the ones before still get wrong. 3 stumps.
10 stumps: the residuals shrink.
60 stumps: a close fit built from very simple pieces. Boosting lowers bias; too many steps would start fitting the noise, so watch validation error.

f2-t12.title: Support vector machines: the widest street between the classes

frames.caption: Two classes that a straight line can separate. But many lines would work. Which is best?
This line separates them, but it passes very close to some points. A slightly different new point could land on the wrong side.
An SVM picks the line with the widest empty street (the margin) between the classes.
Only the points touching the edges of the street matter: the support vectors (yellow rings). Move any other point a little and the line doesn't change.
The hinge loss is max(0, 1 − y·score), with labels y = ±1. A point on the right side, past the margin (y·score = 2): loss 0.
Right side but inside the margin (y·score = 0.5): loss 0.5. The SVM still pushes it out.
Wrong side (y·score = −1): loss 2, growing in a straight line the further it is. A soft-margin SVM balances these losses against a wide margin, using C.

f2-t13.title: Naive Bayes: each word adds its own evidence

frames.caption: Before reading any words: 40% of all email is spam, so the prior is 40% spam, 60% ham (not spam).
"free" appears in 30% of spam but only 2% of ham. Multiply each side by its probability: 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12 against 0.6 × 0.02 = 0.012. Now 91% spam.
"prize": 0.1 against 0.005. Multiply again. Treating each word as separate evidence is the "naive" part. Now 99.5% spam.
"today" is equally common in both (0.05), so it changes nothing. Real filters add logs instead of multiplying, so long emails don't round to 0.

f2-t14.title: k-means: assign to the nearest centre, move the centre, repeat

frames.caption: 36 unlabelled points. Choose k = 3 and drop three centres (stars) at poor starting places.
Assign: each point joins its nearest centre and takes its colour.
Move: each centre jumps to the average of its points.
Round 2, assign again: some points switch to a closer centre.
Round 2, move the centres again.
Round 3, assign again: some points switch to a closer centre.
Round 3, move the centres again.
Round 4, assign again: some points switch to a closer centre.
Round 4, move the centres again.
Repeat until nothing changes. The centres settle in the middle of the three groups. A different start can settle somewhere worse, so run it several times (or use k-means++).

f2-t15.title: Choosing how many components to keep, and when PCA hurts

frames.caption: Data with 8 features. PCA's first component alone holds 53% of the variance.
The rest hold less and less. This is a scree plot: share of variance per component.
Add them up (green). 4 components reach the 95% line, so you can keep 4 numbers per sample instead of 8 and lose only 5% of the spread.
Two classes, blue and pink. They differ only in the up–down direction, which has small spread. Most of the spread is left–right.
PCA ignores the labels and keeps the direction with the most spread: left–right.
Squash onto that one component and the two classes land on top of each other. The useful direction was thrown away. PCA keeps spread, not usefulness.

f2-t16.title: EM: guess who belongs where, refit, repeat

frames.caption: Delivery times from two routes, but nobody recorded which route. Start with two bell curves in rough, wrong places.
E-step: for each point, how much does each curve explain it? Colour shows the share: blue for curve 1, pink for curve 2, purple for "a bit of both".
M-step: refit each curve as a weighted average of the points, using those shares as weights. The log-likelihood goes up.
Round 2, E-step: recompute every point's shares.
Round 2, M-step: the curves move again, and the fit improves again.
Round 3, E-step: recompute every point's shares.
Round 3, M-step: the curves move again, and the fit improves again.
Converged: one route around 20 minutes (60% of deliveries), the other around 46 (40%). Found without ever being told which route a delivery took.

f2-t17.title: Capacity and the surprise of double descent

frames.caption: Capacity: how many points can a model separate in every possible way? Three points, all one colour: any line that leaves them on one side works.
One different from the other two: a line can cut it off.
Any single point can be cut off like this.
All 8 labellings of 3 points can be separated by some line. Lines "shatter" 3 points.
Four points in the XOR pattern: diagonal pairs share a colour. No straight line can separate them. So the VC dimension of a line in 2-D is 3.
Illustration: test error as a model gets more features (parameters), trained on 100 points. Classical regime first.
Classical U-shape: error falls, then rises as the model starts fitting noise. At 100 features (= 100 training points) it can fit them exactly, and error spikes.
Keep growing, and test error falls again, below the classical best. This second descent is "double descent", seen in linear models and deep networks alike.

f3-t1.title: A neuron, and many neurons stacked in layers

frames.caption: One neuron. Three inputs arrive (features, or the outputs of the layer before).
Each input has its own weight. Green weights push the output up, pink ones push it down; thicker means bigger.
Multiply each input by its weight: 0.4, 0.4, 1.2.
Add them up, plus the bias (-0.5): z = w·x + b = 1.5.
Apply the activation: ReLU(z) = max(0, 1.5) = 1.5. That one number is the neuron's output. Logistic regression is exactly this, with a sigmoid instead of ReLU.
A multi-layer perceptron (MLP): layers of neurons, each fully connected to the next. The input layer holds the features.
Hidden layer 1: every neuron does w·x + b and a ReLU, all at once. In code that is one matrix multiply: h = relu(x @ W1 + b1).
Hidden layer 2 takes layer 1's outputs as its inputs, and does the same.
The output layer gives one score per class (no ReLU here). This left-to-right pass is the forward pass. Training will adjust every weight on every line.

f3-t2.title: Activation functions: the bends that let networks learn curves

frames.caption: ReLU: zero for negative inputs, the input itself for positive ones. Cheap, and its slope is exactly 1 when active, so gradients pass through. The default choice.
Sigmoid: squashes everything into 0 to 1. Its slope is at most 0.25 and almost 0 at both ends, so deep stacks of sigmoids make gradients vanish. Used for gates and yes/no outputs.
tanh: like the sigmoid but from −1 to 1, and centred on 0. Used inside RNNs and LSTMs.
GELU: a smooth ReLU that lets small negatives through a little. Transformers use it (or close relatives like SiLU).
Why non-linearity? Without it, layer after layer of matrices collapses into one matrix: a straight line can never become the curve (dashed).
Add one ReLU unit: max(0, x − 1.6) adds a single bend (orange dot). The output is now two straight pieces.
Four ReLUs, four bends. Each hidden neuron adds one hinge where it switches on.
Thirteen ReLUs: almost indistinguishable from the curve. With enough neurons, a network can approximate almost any shape. That is the universal approximation idea.

f3-t3.title: Backpropagation: values go forward, blame flows back

frames.caption: Start with weight w = 1, input x = 2 and target y = 5.
Forward: ŷ = w·x = 2.
L = e² = 9. Now go backwards to find dL/dw.
Start at the end: dL/dL = 1.

shapes.text: each step: gradient from the right × local derivative

frames.caption: L = e², so its local derivative is 2e = -6. Gradient so far: 1 × -6 = -6.

shapes.text: each step: gradient from the right × local derivative

frames.caption: e = ŷ − y, so de/dŷ = 1. Pass -6 × 1 = -6 back to ŷ.

shapes.text: each step: gradient from the right × local derivative

frames.caption: ŷ = w·x, so dŷ/dw = x = 2. dL/dw = -6 × 2 = -12. Negative, so increasing w lowers the loss. That is all backprop is: local derivatives multiplied from the end backwards.

shapes.text: each step: gradient from the right × local derivative

f3-t4.title: Autograd records a graph forwards, then walks it backwards

frames.caption: Two inputs that need gradients: a = 2 and b = −3.
Compute e = a × b. Autograd quietly records the operation and its inputs: a node in the graph.
d = e + c: another node, another edge.
L = d × f = −8. The whole calculation is now a graph. Every value is kept in memory for the backward pass.
loss.backward() starts at L with gradient 1…
…through ×: d gets f = −2 and f gets d = 4 (each side gets the other side's value).
Through +: the gradient is passed on unchanged, so e and c both get −2.
Through × again: a gets −2 × b = 6, b gets −2 × a = −4. Every .grad is filled in, with no calculus done by hand.

f3-t5.title: Softmax turns scores into probabilities; cross-entropy scores them

frames.caption: The network's last layer gives raw scores, called logits: 2, 1 and 0.1. They are not probabilities: they can be negative and don't add up to 1.
Exponentiate each: e² = 7.39, e¹ = 2.72, e⁰·¹ = 1.11. Everything is now positive, and the leader pulls further ahead.
Divide by the total (11.21): 0.66, 0.24, 0.1. These are probabilities that add up to 1. That is softmax.
The true answer is "cat". Cross-entropy loss = −log(p_cat) = −log 0.66 = 0.42.
And the gradient of the loss with respect to the logits is simply p − y: [-0.34, 0.24, 0.1]. Push the cat score up, the others down.

f3-t6.title: SGD, momentum and Adam racing down a narrow valley

frames.caption: A long, narrow valley: steep across, gentle along. All three optimisers start at the same point (left) and aim for the yellow minimum.
SGD (red) bounces across the steep walls, because the gradient points mostly across the valley, not along it.
Momentum (orange) averages its recent steps: the side-to-side parts cancel and speed builds up along the valley.

Adam (green) scales each direction by its typical gradient size, so its path is straighter early on. Here all three end near the bottom, but only because SGD's learning rate was set just under the value where it would blow up. Adam works well across many problems with little tuning, which is why AdamW is the usual default.
A learning-rate schedule changes the step size during training. Plot learning rate (as a share of its peak) against training step.
Warm-up: start tiny and ramp up over the first steps, while Adam's running averages are still unreliable and the weights are random.
Then cosine decay: big steps early to make progress, small steps late to settle into a good minimum. Warm-up then cosine is the standard recipe for transformers.

f3-t7.title: Keeping the signal the same size through many layers

frames.caption: A 16-layer ReLU network. Each bar will show how big the activations are at that layer, on a log scale; 1 (dashed) is healthy.
Weights with std 0.01: every layer shrinks the signal. By layer 16 it is about 8e-22: it has vanished, and so will the gradients on the way back.
Same network, same input.
He initialisation, std = √(2 / 48): each layer keeps the signal about the same size, layer after layer. The extra 2 makes up for ReLU zeroing half the values.
Same network, same input.
Weights with std 1: every layer multiplies the signal by about √(48/2) ≈ 4.9. By layer 16 it is about 8e+10: exploding, and soon inf or NaN.

f3-t8.title: Normalising activations: down the batch, or across the features

frames.caption: A batch of 4 examples (rows), each with 5 features (columns). Feature 2 is large and feature 5 is small: very different scales.
Batch norm works down each column: for one feature, take its mean and spread across the batch.
Every column now has mean 0 and spread 1 (orange above the mean, purple below). The network then rescales each feature with learned γ and β.
Because the statistics come from the batch, batch norm needs a decent batch size, and at test time it uses running averages saved during training.
The same batch.
Layer norm works across each row: for one example, take the mean and spread over its own features.
Every row now has mean 0 and spread 1. Each example is normalised on its own, so the batch size doesn't matter and training and test behave the same. That is why transformers use layer norm.
A network with two hidden layers.

shapes.text: test time: every unit on, no scaling

frames.caption: Training step 1, dropout rate 0.5: a random half of the hidden neurons are switched off (red). The rest are scaled up × 2 so the total signal stays the same size.

shapes.text: training: random half of hidden units dropped, survivors × 2

frames.caption: Step 2: a different random half. No neuron can rely on any particular partner being there, so each must learn something useful on its own.

shapes.text: training: random half of hidden units dropped, survivors × 2

frames.caption: Step 3: another random team. In effect, you train a huge number of thinned networks that share weights.

shapes.text: training: random half of hidden units dropped, survivors × 2

frames.caption: At test time dropout is off: every neuron is used, with no scaling (that is why it was scaled during training). Forgetting model.eval() leaves dropout on, and predictions become random.

shapes.text: test time: every unit on, no scaling

frames.caption: One training image. A model trained on only this exact picture can memorise its pixels.
Data augmentation makes new, still-correct examples: flip it, and it is still the same kind of thing.
Shift or crop it, and it is still the same thing too. Each epoch the model sees a slightly different version, so memorising pixels stops working and it must learn the shape.

f3-t10.title: The training loop: the same six steps, every batch

frames.caption: The DataLoader hands over the next shuffled mini-batch: inputs xb and labels yb.
Forward pass: run the batch through the model to get logits. Autograd records the graph as it goes.
Compute the loss: one number saying how wrong this batch was.
Clear the old gradients. PyTorch adds new gradients to old ones, so skipping this mixes batches together.
Backward pass: autograd fills in .grad for every weight.
The optimiser updates every weight using its gradient. Then back to the top for the next batch — thousands of times.

f3-t11.title: Convolution: one small filter slid across the whole image

frames.caption: A tiny grey-scale image: dark on top (0), bright below (9). And a 3 × 3 filter that responds to "dark above, bright below": a horizontal edge.
Place the filter on the top-left 3 × 3 patch, multiply matching numbers and add them up: all dark, so 0.
Slide across the top row (all 0), then down one row. Now the bottom of the window covers bright pixels: 9 + 9 + 9 = 27. A strong response: an edge!
One more row down: dark in the top row of the window, bright in the bottom row. Again 27.
All bright: the −1s and +1s cancel to 0. The finished feature map lights up exactly along the edge.
Output size = (W − K + 2P)/S + 1 = (6 − 3 + 0)/1 + 1 = 4. The same 9 weights were reused at every position, so an edge is found anywhere in the picture. A real layer learns dozens of filters at once.
The receptive field is how much of the original image one output value can "see".
After one 3 × 3 convolution, each output sees a 3 × 3 patch: enough for an edge.
Stack a second 3 × 3 layer: each output now sees 5 × 5, because each of its 9 inputs saw its own 3 × 3.
Three layers: 7 × 7. Deeper layers see bigger regions, so they can recognise bigger things: edges, then corners, then eyes, then faces. Pooling and stride grow it faster.

f3-t12.title: Residual connections: a shortcut for the signal and the gradient

frames.caption: A plain deep network: each block transforms its input, y = F(x). The gradient has to pass back through every block.
Illustration: if each block shrinks the gradient to about half on the way back, early layers (left) get almost nothing. They barely learn.
A residual block adds its input back: y = x + F(x). The block only has to learn the change, and an identity "highway" (green) runs past every block.
The derivative of x + F(x) is 1 + F′(x). That "1" carries the gradient straight back, so early layers still learn. This is what made 50-, 100- and 1,000-layer networks trainable.

f3-t13.title: An RNN reads one step at a time, with a fading memory

frames.caption: An RNN reads "the cat" one character at a time. After "t", the hidden state h₁ (its memory) is all about "t".

shapes.text: colour = how much of each letter the memory still holds

frames.caption: Each step mixes the new character into the memory using the same weights: hₜ = tanh(W·hₜ₋₁ + U·xₜ). Older characters take up less and less room.

shapes.text: colour = how much of each letter the memory still holds

frames.caption: By the last "t", the first "t" is a thin sliver. Information from far back fades, because it has been squeezed through the same small memory again and again.

shapes.text: colour = how much of each letter the memory still holds

frames.caption: Training has the same problem in reverse: the gradient to early steps is multiplied by W at every step. If that factor is 0.9, after 100 steps it is 0.9¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.00003: vanished. LSTMs and then transformers were invented to fix this.

shapes.text: colour = how much of each letter the memory still holds

f3-t14.title: Embeddings: a learned vector for every item

frames.caption: An embedding layer is just a table: one row of numbers per item in the vocabulary. Here, 5 words × 6 numbers.
The word "cat" has id 1. Its embedding is simply row 1 of the table: a lookup, no maths.
The rows are ordinary weights. When a sentence uses "cat", backprop only changes row 1, nudging it to be more useful. Over many sentences, similar words drift close together.
Each word gets a vector, shown here in 2-D. Before training the vectors are random, so the map means nothing.
Training nudges the vectors so words used in similar ways end up close: fruit near fruit, pets near pets, royalty near people.
Directions can carry meaning too: man → king is roughly the same arrow as woman → queen. So king − man + woman lands near queen.

f3-t15.title: Two checks that catch most training bugs

variants.label: Step-0 loss and overfit one batch

frames.caption: Check 1, before any training: with 10 classes and random weights, every class gets about 1/10, so the loss should be −ln(1/10) = ln 10 ≈ 2.3.
If step 0 shows something like 15 (far off the top), the outputs are wildly over-confident: bad initialisation, or a softmax/loss bug. Fix it before training.
Check 2: train on one small batch only. A working model should drive its loss close to 0 by memorising it.
If it can't (the loss stalls, red), there is a bug: labels misaligned, gradients not flowing, or the optimiser not stepping. Only once this works, train on everything.

f3-t16.title: An LSTM cell: a memory belt with three gates

frames.caption: The cell state is a conveyor belt of memory running through time. It arrives holding 0.8.
Forget gate: a number from 0 to 1 decides how much to keep. f = 0.9, so 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72 stays.
Input gate and new content: add i × g = 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.3. The belt now holds 1.02. The memory is updated by adding, not by repeated multiplying, so gradients can travel far back along the belt.
Output gate: what to reveal this step. h = o × tanh(c) = 0.7 × 0.77 = 0.54. A GRU does the same job with two gates instead of three.

f4-t1.title: Byte-pair encoding: merge the most common pair, again and again

frames.caption: Start with single characters. "low", "lower" and "lowest" are 3, 5 and 6 tokens long.
Count every neighbouring pair. "l"+"o" appears 3 times (tied with "o"+"w", so the first one wins). Merge it into one new token, "lo".
Count again. Now "lo"+"w" is most common: merge into "low". The vocabulary grows by one token per merge.
"low"+"e" appears twice: merge into "lowe". Common pieces become single tokens.
One more merge gives "lower". Real tokenizers do tens of thousands of merges on huge text, so common words become one token and rare words split into pieces.

shapes.text: new tokens: lo, low, lowe, lower

frames.caption: Each token id becomes a vector (shown as a column of colours). "dog" always gets the same vector, wherever it appears.
"man bites dog" uses exactly the same three vectors. Attention on its own treats the input as a bag of vectors, so it can't tell these two sentences apart.
Add a position vector for seat 0, 1, 2. Now "dog" in seat 0 and "dog" in seat 2 look different, and word order is part of the input.
Sinusoidal position encoding: one row per position (top to bottom), one column per dimension.
Each column is a wave. The first columns change quickly from row to row; later columns change slowly.

Together the waves give every position a unique pattern, like a binary clock with smooth hands, and nearby positions get similar patterns. Many modern models use RoPE instead, which rotates queries and keys by an angle that depends on position.

f4-t3.title: Self-attention: each word gathers information from the words it needs

frames.caption: A sentence. To understand "it", the model needs to know what "it" refers to.
"it" makes a query (what am I looking for?). Every word makes a key (what do I contain?). Score = query · key / √d for each word. (Scores here are an illustration of what a trained model learns.)
Softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to 1. "animal" gets 0.55, the biggest share.
Drawn as lines: thicker means more attention. "it" looks mostly at "animal", a little at "tired".

The output for "it" is the weighted average of every word's value vector, so "it" now carries information about the animal. Every word does this at the same time, in parallel: one matrix multiply, Q·Kᵀ, then softmax, then times V.

f4-t4.title: Many heads, one block, stacked many times

frames.caption: Multi-head attention runs several attentions side by side. (Illustration: real heads learn their own, often messier, patterns.)
head 1: previous word: each word attends to the word just before it.
head 2: who did what: "paid" looks at who paid and who was paid.
head 3: money and dates: "paid" looks at the amount and the day.
Each head works in its own smaller space (768 dimensions split into 12 heads of 64 in GPT-2 small). Their outputs are joined back together and mixed by one more matrix.
A transformer block. Each token's vector flows along the residual stream (blue), left to right.
Layer norm, then multi-head attention: tokens exchange information with each other.
The result is added back onto the stream: x = x + attention(LN(x)). A residual connection.
Layer norm again, then an MLP applied to each token on its own (usually 4× wider inside). Attention moves information between tokens; the MLP processes it within each token.
Added back again: x = x + MLP(LN(x)). A model like GPT-2 small stacks 12 of these blocks, all the same shape.

f4-t5.title: GPT: predict the next token, append it, repeat

frames.caption: A GPT reads the text so far, "The cat sat on the" …
… and outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary (the top 5 shown). Probabilities here are an illustration.
Pick one (here the likeliest, "mat") and append it. Now the input is one token longer: predict again.
Predict, append, repeat. That is all generation is. Each new token can only look at tokens before it, enforced by the causal mask.
The causal mask: row = the token doing the looking, column = the token being looked at.
Green cells are allowed, red are blocked (set to −∞ before the softmax). Each token sees itself and everything before it, never the future.
This makes training efficient: one pass over "The cat sat on the mat" trains 5 predictions at once: The → cat, The cat → sat, and so on. The targets are the inputs shifted left by one.

shapes.text:
input:
The cat sat on the

target:
cat sat on the mat

f4-t6.title: Encoders look both ways; decoders only look back

frames.caption: Encoder (BERT): every token can attend to every other token, before and after it. Fully green.
Decoder (GPT): each token sees only itself and the past. The upper triangle is blocked.
BERT is trained on fill-in-the-blank: some tokens are hidden and it must guess them.
To fill [MASK], it uses words on both sides, including "of France" after the gap. That two-way view makes encoders strong for understanding: classification, search embeddings.
A GPT predicting the word after "Paris is the" may only look left. One-way view, but it can generate text one token at a time. Today most big models are decoders.

f4-t13.title: Images as sequences of patches, and pictures matched to words

frames.caption: A vision transformer starts from an ordinary image.
Cut it into square patches, for example 16 × 16 pixels each. Here a 4 × 4 grid of patches.
Lay the patches out in a row, like words in a sentence. Each patch is flattened and turned into a vector by one linear layer: a patch embedding.
Add position embeddings (patch 5 must know it sits at row 1, column 1), then run an ordinary transformer. A 224 × 224 image with 16 × 16 patches gives 196 tokens.
CLIP has two encoders: one for images, one for text. Each maps its input to a vector in the same space.
Each cell is the similarity (dot product) between an image's vector and a caption's vector. Before training, it is noise.
Training pushes each matching pair (the diagonal) together and every mismatch apart, over hundreds of millions of image–caption pairs. (Numbers are an illustration.)
Zero-shot classification: embed a new photo, embed the texts "a photo of a cat", "a photo of a dog", …, and pick the closest. No cat-versus-dog training needed.

f4-t7.title: Choosing the next token: temperature, top-k and top-p

frames.caption: Next-token probabilities at temperature 1: "mat" 0.52, and a long tail of less likely words.
Temperature 0.5 divides the logits by 0.5 before softmax: the top choice grows to 0.78. Sharper, safer, more repetitive.
Temperature 2: flatter. "mat" falls to 0.34 and even "moon" gets 0.06. More creative, more mistakes.
Temperature near 0 is greedy decoding: always the single most likely token. Deterministic, but prone to dull loops.
Start from the full distribution (T = 1).
Top-k with k = 3: keep only the 3 most likely tokens and drop the rest.
Renormalise the survivors so they add up to 1 again, then sample. Strange low-probability words can never appear.

Top-p (nucleus) with p = 0.9: keep the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least 0.9 — here 4 tokens. When the model is sure, the set is small; when it is unsure, it is larger.

f4-t8.title: The KV cache: remember keys and values instead of recomputing them

frames.caption: Generating token by token. Each new token's attention needs the keys (K) and values (V) of every earlier token.
Without a cache, step 2 recomputes K and V for all 2 tokens (red = recomputed, again).
Without a cache, step 3 recomputes K and V for all 3 tokens (red = recomputed, again).
After 6 tokens: 21 K,V computations, growing with the square of the length. For a long reply that is hopelessly wasteful.
With a KV cache: compute K and V for each token once, and store them.
Step 2: only the new token's K and V are computed (yellow); the rest are read from memory.
Step 3: only the new token's K and V are computed (yellow); the rest are read from memory.
After 6 tokens: 6 computations instead of 21. The price is memory: 2 × layers × tokens × d_model × bytes. For 32 layers, d_model 4,096, 4,096 tokens in bf16 that is about 2.1 GB per sequence.

f4-t9.title: Scaling laws: bigger models, more data, predictably lower loss

frames.caption: Illustration. Train a small model and record its final loss and the compute it used.
Train bigger models on more data with more compute. Each one reaches a lower loss.
On log scales the points fall on a smooth curve (a power law). You can fit it on small runs and predict the loss of a run 100 times bigger before paying for it.

Chinchilla's finding: for a fixed compute budget, grow parameters and training tokens together — about 20 tokens per parameter. A 1B model "wants" about 20B tokens. Many modern models train far longer, because smaller models are cheaper to serve.

f4-t12.title: Mixture of experts: many experts, only a few used per token

frames.caption: A mixture-of-experts layer replaces one big MLP with many expert MLPs (8 here) and a small router.
The router scores every expert for the token "The" and keeps the top 2: E2 and E7. Only those two run.
"tax" goes to a different pair: E4 and E3. Each token uses only 2 of 8 experts' worth of compute.
After all 6 tokens, expert usage is 0, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 0. A load-balancing loss keeps this even, so no expert is overloaded or starved. Every expert must still sit in memory, used or not.

f4-t10.title: LoRA: freeze the big matrix, train a tiny low-rank update

frames.caption: A pretrained weight matrix W. In a real model it might be 4,096 × 4,096: 16.8 million numbers. Full fine-tuning would update every one.
LoRA freezes W. Instead it adds two thin matrices: B (tall, r columns) and A (wide, r rows), with a small rank r such as 8.
B × A is a full-size matrix, but it is built from far fewer numbers: for 4,096 × 4,096 and r = 8, only 65,536 trainable weights, about 0.4%.
The layer uses W + B·A. B starts at zero, so training begins from exactly the pretrained model. Afterwards the small adapter can be saved, swapped or merged into W.

f4-t11.title: From text predictor to helpful assistant

frames.caption: A pretrained model only continues text. Ask it a question and it might write five more questions.
Instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning): train on thousands of example conversations, so it learns to answer helpfully in a chat format.
Collect preference data: for one prompt, two answers, and a person (or model) marks which is better.
RLHF: train a reward model to score answers like the human did, then use reinforcement learning (PPO) to make the model produce high-scoring answers, without drifting too far from the original.
DPO skips the reward model: it adjusts the model directly so the chosen answer becomes more likely than the rejected one. Simpler, and now very common.

f4-t14.title: Thinking longer: chains of thought and majority votes

frames.caption: Asked to answer at once, a model may pattern-match ("3 … 2 … 12") and blurt out a wrong number.

shapes.text: A shop sells pens at 3 for £2. How much do 12 pens cost?

frames.caption: A reasoning model first writes out intermediate steps: a chain of thought. Each step is a smaller, easier prediction.

shapes.text: A shop sells pens at 3 for £2. How much do 12 pens cost?

frames.caption: With the steps written down, the final answer follows from them. Spending more tokens on thinking is spending more test-time compute.

shapes.text: A shop sells pens at 3 for £2. How much do 12 pens cost?

frames.caption: Self-consistency: sample a full chain of thought several times with some randomness (temperature above 0).

shapes.text: A shop sells pens at 3 for £2. How much do 12 pens cost?

frames.caption: Different paths sometimes reach different answers. Individual samples can be wrong.

shapes.text: A shop sells pens at 3 for £2. How much do 12 pens cost?

frames.caption: After 10 samples, take a majority vote: £8 wins with 7 of 10. Correct reasoning paths tend to agree; wrong ones scatter. The cost is 10 times the tokens.

shapes.text: A shop sells pens at 3 for £2. How much do 12 pens cost?

f5-t1.title: A good prompt is a complete briefing

frames.caption: A weak prompt, "Summarise this.", leaves the model guessing: how long, for whom, in what format? It guesses, and code can't read the result.

shapes.text: "Sure! This ticket seems to be about some kind of issue…"  ✗

frames.caption: Start with a role and the context the model can't know: who it is helping and where the text comes from.

shapes.text: Role: you are a support triage assistant.
Context: tickets come from our billing app.

frames.caption: State the task precisely: what to do, how long, and for whom.

shapes.text: Role: you are a support triage assistant.
Context: tickets come from our billing app.
Task: summarise in 2 sentences for an engineer.

frames.caption: Show an example of exactly the output you want. Examples are often worth more than paragraphs of rules.

shapes.text: Role: you are a support triage assistant.
Context: tickets come from our billing app.
Task: summarise in 2 sentences for an engineer.

frames.caption: Ask for a fixed format when code will read the answer. Now the reply is short, correct and machine-readable. Measure it on many inputs, not one.

shapes.text: Role: you are a support triage assistant.
Context: tickets come from our billing app.
Task: summarise in 2 sentences for an engineer.

f5-t10.title: Function calling: the model asks, your code acts

frames.caption: The user asks a question that needs live data the model doesn't have.
Your app sends the question plus a description of the available tools: their names and a JSON schema for their arguments.
Instead of answering in prose, the model replies with a structured tool call: which tool, with which arguments. Your code can parse it reliably.
Your code (not the model) runs the function. Validate the arguments first.
The tool returns data.
Your app sends the result back to the model as a tool result message.
Now the model writes the final answer from real data. This loop can repeat for several tool calls.

f5-t2.title: Semantic search: nearest meaning, not matching words

frames.caption: An embedding model turns each help article into a vector (shown in 2-D). Articles about the same thing land close together, even with different words.
The user types "can't sign in". It shares no words with "I forgot my login", but it is embedded with the same model into the same space.
Find the closest vectors (by cosine similarity): the three login articles. That is semantic search: matching meaning, not keywords.
Its weakness: an exact code like "SKU-4471" has little meaning to embed, so a query for it may land nowhere near. Hybrid search adds keyword matching and combines the scores.

f5-t11.title: Approximate nearest-neighbour search: hop through a graph instead of checking everything

frames.caption: An HNSW index links vectors into a graph with several layers. Search starts at an entry point on the sparse top layer and hops to whichever neighbour is closer to the query (yellow).

shapes.text: top layer: few points, long links

frames.caption: When no neighbour is closer, drop to the next, denser layer and keep hopping from there. Like zooming in on a map.

On the bottom layer, the walk ends next to the query, close to (but not exactly at) the true nearest vector. Only a handful of the 60 vectors were compared, instead of all of them. With millions of vectors that is the difference between milliseconds and seconds, at the price of occasionally missing the true best match.
Offline, once: start from your documents — manuals, policies, notes.
Split them into chunks of a few hundred words, with a little overlap, so each chunk is about one thing.
Embed every chunk and store the vectors in an index, with metadata like source and date.
At question time: embed the user's question with the same embedding model.
Retrieve the chunks whose vectors are closest to the question (say the top 5, or more).
Optionally re-rank: a slower, more careful model re-orders the candidates by true relevance.
Build the prompt: instructions, the best chunks marked as data, and the question. "Answer only from these sources; cite them; say if the answer isn't there." The LLM writes a grounded answer.

f5-t12.title: Context engineering: choose what goes in the window

frames.caption: A context window of 32,000 tokens: everything the model sees on one call.
A deliberate budget: instructions, a few examples, the 3 most relevant documents, a running summary plus the last 5 messages, and room left for the answer.
Stuffing in 50 documents and all 200 past messages overflows the window, and long before that it gets slower, costs more and usually answers worse.
Illustration of the "lost in the middle" finding: models use facts at the start and end of a long context more reliably than facts buried in the middle. Put what matters where it will be used.

shapes.text: position of the fact in the context

f5-t4.title: Evaluation: measure, then read the failures

frames.caption: An eval set: 50 real questions with expected answers. Run the whole app on all of them.
Score each one: code checks where possible (does the JSON parse? is the number right?), an LLM judge where you must. 31 of 50 pass.
Now the most valuable step: read every failure and label why it failed. Group them.
12 of the 19 failures retrieved the wrong chunk. So fix retrieval first, not the prompt. Error analysis tells you where to spend effort.
After improving retrieval, rerun the same 50 questions: 43 pass. Same test set, so the comparison is fair. Keep adding new failure cases from real use.

f5-t5.title: An agent: think, act, observe, repeat

frames.caption: Task: "How many days from 3 March to the 2026 ML conference?" An agent is a model in a loop with tools.
Think: the model decides it needs the conference date and chooses the search tool.
Act: your code runs the tool call.
Observe: the result goes back into the context: "12 June 2026".
Not done yet. Think again: now it needs date arithmetic, so it calls the calculator: days between 3 March and 12 June.
Observe 101 days, decide it is done, and answer. Real agents need a step limit, error handling for failing tools, and logs of every step, because loops can go wrong silently.

f5-t13.title: MCP: one standard plug between AI apps and tools

frames.caption: An AI app (the host) contains an MCP client. It can connect to any number of MCP servers, each written once and usable by any MCP-speaking app.
On connect, each server lists what it offers: tools (actions), resources (data) and prompts. The user asks "what did I write about LoRA?", and the model chooses search_notes.
The client sends the call to the notes server, which runs it and returns the results.
The results go back into the model's context and it answers. Because servers can read data and take actions, connect only servers you trust, and treat their outputs as untrusted data.

f5-t6.title: Prompt first, RAG for knowledge, fine-tune for behaviour

frames.caption: Always start with prompting: it is cheapest and fastest to change. Measure it with your evals before reaching for more.

shapes.text:
Need a behaviour or format
prompts can't make reliable?

frames.caption: "Answer questions from our 2026 price list": the model doesn't know your prices, and they change. That is missing knowledge → RAG.

shapes.text:
Need a behaviour or format
prompts can't make reliable?
case: answer from our price list → RAG

frames.caption: "Always reply in our strict legal-letter format": a behaviour. Try a prompt with examples; only if it keeps failing, fine-tune.

shapes.text:
Need a behaviour or format
prompts can't make reliable?

frames.caption: "Answer questions about a customer's own orders": every customer has different, changing data. That is knowledge to look up at question time → RAG, or a database tool. They also combine: a fine-tuned model can still use RAG.

frames.caption: Start from 5,000 historical support replies. Some are excellent, many are not.
Remove exact and near duplicates: the model would otherwise over-learn the most repeated replies.
Filter for quality: drop wrong, rude, outdated or off-policy replies. A model copies every example, mistakes included.
Balance across topics, so billing questions don't drown out everything else.
Hold back 50 examples the model never trains on, for honest testing. 400 excellent examples often beat 5,000 messy ones.

f5-t7.title: Serving a model: API, container, batching

frames.caption: Serving means putting the model behind an API. A client sends a request…
…a web framework like FastAPI receives it, validates the input and logs it. A /health endpoint lets the platform check the service is alive.
The model generates the answer. Measure latency (time to first token, then tokens per second) and cost per request.
Docker packages the code, the model files and every dependency into one image, so it runs the same on your laptop and in the cloud.
Under load, handling one request at a time leaves the GPU mostly idle while users queue.

shapes.text: one at a time: each waits for the last

frames.caption: Model servers batch requests together: one GPU pass serves several users. Throughput goes up a lot; each user may wait slightly longer. Continuous batching (vLLM and others) adds new requests as old ones finish.

shapes.text: batched: 4 requests share one GPU pass

f5-t15.title: Cutting cost: cache what repeats, route what is easy

frames.caption: Sending every request to the biggest model is simple but expensive: each costs 10 units here.
12 requests, 120 units.

Add a cache: an exact repeat (or, carefully, a near-identical question) is answered from stored results for almost nothing. Then a router sends easy requests to a small model costing 1 unit and hard ones to the big model.

Same 12 requests: 27 units instead of 120. In general, if 70% of traffic can use a model costing a tenth as much, routing alone saves about 63%. Check quality with evals so the savings don't hide worse answers.

f5-t16.title: Tracing: see every step of a single request

frames.caption: A trace records one request as a tree of steps (spans), each with its inputs, outputs, time, tokens and cost.
Drawn as a waterfall, the LLM call dominates the 2.4 seconds. That tells you where speed work would pay off.
A user complains the bot quoted the wrong refund policy. Open that request's trace and inspect each span's output.
The retrieval span ranked an outdated 2023 policy first. The bug is in retrieval (add a date filter), not in the prompt. Turn this case into a new eval question so it stays fixed.
