f5-t9.title: ML systems: the loop around the model, and drift

frames.caption: A real ML system is a loop, not a model: collect data, label it, build features…
…train and evaluate, then serve predictions. Training-serving skew happens when production computes features differently from training: share one feature pipeline.
Monitor inputs, predictions and outcomes, then retrain when the world changes. Most of the work, and most failures, are outside the model.
Training data (blue): a feature, say transaction amount, as it looked in 2024.
Live data in 2026 (pink) has shifted: fraudsters changed tactics. The model was never trained on this region, so its precision quietly drops.
Monitoring compares live inputs and outcomes with training data and raises an alert when they diverge. Then retrain on recent, correctly labelled data.

f6-t1.title: Thousands of fast cores, one narrow road to memory

frames.caption: A GPU has thousands of simple cores that do the same operation on lots of numbers at once. The numbers live in GPU memory and must travel to the cores.
Adding two vectors: load 2 numbers, do 1 addition, store 1. The cores finish instantly and then wait for the next numbers. Most of the GPU sits idle: memory-bound.
A big matrix multiply reuses every number loaded many times, so the cores stay busy while data trickles in: compute-bound. This is what GPUs are built for.
Illustration: a roofline. Low arithmetic intensity (few FLOPs per byte) is limited by memory bandwidth, so speed rises with intensity…

shapes.text: arithmetic intensity: FLOPs per byte moved (log)

frames.caption: …until the flat roof: past the ridge point, the GPU's maths is the limit. Vector add sits far down the slope.

shapes.text: arithmetic intensity: FLOPs per byte moved (log)

frames.caption: Softmax is still memory-bound; a big matmul reaches the compute roof. Speed-ups come from moving fewer bytes (fusion, lower precision) or doing more maths per byte.

shapes.text: arithmetic intensity: FLOPs per byte moved (log)

f6-t2.title: fp32, fp16 and bf16: the same number in fewer bits

frames.caption: fp32 uses 32 bits: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits (how big or small the number can be) and 23 mantissa bits (how many significant digits).
fp16 halves the memory: 5 exponent bits, 10 mantissa bits. Good precision, but its largest value is only about 65,504, so big gradients overflow to inf and tiny ones underflow to 0.
bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits (range up to about 3.4 × 10³⁸) and keeps only 7 mantissa bits. Overflow is rare; the cost is coarse precision: in bf16, 1 + 0.001 rounds back to 1.

Mixed precision does the heavy matrix maths in 16-bit (half the memory traffic, much faster on tensor cores) but keeps a 32-bit master copy of the weights and does the optimiser update in fp32, so small updates aren't rounded away. bf16 is the usual choice today.

f6-t3.title: Where training memory goes: about 16 bytes per parameter

frames.caption: Inference only needs the weights: 2 bytes per parameter in bf16. A 1-billion-parameter model needs about 2 GB.
Training also stores a gradient for every weight: 2 more bytes.
Mixed precision keeps an fp32 master copy of the weights, so tiny updates aren't rounded away: 4 more.
Adam keeps two running averages per weight, each in fp32: 8 more. Total about 16 bytes per parameter, so 1B parameters need about 16 GB before activations.

On top come the activations saved for backprop, which grow with batch size and sequence length. Gradient checkpointing, smaller batches with gradient accumulation, and sharding (ZeRO/FSDP) are the usual fixes.

f6-t4.title: Splitting training across GPUs three ways

frames.caption: Data parallel: every GPU holds a full copy of the model.
Each GPU gets a different slice of the batch and computes its own gradients.

An all-reduce averages the gradients across GPUs, so every copy takes the same update and stays identical. Simple and fast, as long as the model fits on one GPU. FSDP/ZeRO go further and shard the weights, gradients and optimiser states.
Tensor parallel: one layer's weight matrix is split across GPUs, here into a left and a right half.
Each GPU multiplies the same input by its half of the matrix.
The half-results are joined. This needs very fast links between GPUs, because they must talk inside every layer, so it is used within one machine.
Pipeline parallel: different layers live on different GPUs, like stations on an assembly line. Micro-batch 1 enters GPU 0.
It moves to GPU 1, and micro-batch 2 enters GPU 0. Splitting the batch into micro-batches keeps more stations busy.
Now 3 GPUs are busy at once.
Full pipeline: all 4 stations work at the same time. At the start and end some stations sit idle (the "bubble"), which is the cost of this method.

f6-t5.title: Faster inference: fewer bits, fewer trips to memory

frames.caption: Some weights of a layer (dots). In bf16 each takes 2 bytes and can be almost any value.
Quantisation keeps only a few allowed levels (dashed lines), spread across the range of the weights, plus one scale factor.
Each weight snaps to its nearest level and is stored as a small integer. Most move only a little, so outputs barely change.

The payoff for a 70-billion-parameter model: about 140 GB in bf16, 70 GB in int8, 35 GB in 4-bit. Less memory and less data to move per token, so faster generation. Always measure quality: at 4 bits and below it can drop.
Standard attention writes the whole T × T score matrix out to GPU memory, then reads it back for the softmax and again for multiplying by V. For long sequences that is a huge amount of traffic.

shapes.text: full T × T matrix, written to HBM

frames.caption: FlashAttention works one tile at a time: load a block of queries, keys and values into the small fast on-chip memory…
…compute that block's scores, softmax and output there, keeping running totals for the softmax, and move on.
The full T × T matrix is never written to slow memory. Same exact result, far fewer bytes moved, and memory grows linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically.

f6-t6.title: Profiling: find where the time really goes

frames.caption: A profiler trace of training steps: what the CPU and the GPU are doing over time.
The GPU (green) is busy only in short bursts. Most of the time it waits while the CPU loads and prepares the next batch. Buying a faster GPU would change nothing.

shapes.text: GPU idle most of the time (red boxes)

frames.caption: Fix the real bottleneck: more DataLoader workers and pinned memory prepare batches in parallel, ahead of time. Now the GPU runs back to back, and 4 steps take less time than 2 did before.

f6-t7.title: Kernel fusion: one trip to memory instead of many

frames.caption: Softmax over a row: find the max, exponentiate and sum, then divide. Each step written as a separate operation is a separate kernel.
Naive version: kernel 1 reads the row from slow memory to find the max.
Kernel 2 reads it again to compute exp(x − max) and the sum, and writes the exponentials back.
Kernel 3 reads the exponentials once more and writes the result. Many trips through the narrow road to memory; the maths itself is cheap.

A fused kernel, written in Triton, loads each row once into fast on-chip memory, does all three steps there, and writes the result once. Same answer, far less memory traffic, so a memory-bound operation runs several times faster.

f6-t8.title: Smaller models: prune what matters little, distil what matters

frames.caption: A layer's weights, coloured by size (brighter = bigger magnitude).
Magnitude pruning: set the smallest 50% of weights to zero (black). Accuracy often barely changes, especially after a little retraining.
Prune 80% and accuracy usually drops more; retraining recovers some. But scattered zeros rarely make the model faster on normal hardware: the matrix is still the same shape.
Structured pruning removes whole rows (neurons), channels or heads instead. The matrix really gets smaller, so it really runs faster.
Distillation trains a small student to copy a big teacher. The usual label for this picture of a "2" is one-hot: 2 = 1, everything else 0.
The teacher's output says more: 2 at 0.90, but 7 at 0.07 and 3 at 0.03. It tells the student that this 2 looks a little like a 7. These soft labels carry extra knowledge.
Dividing the teacher's logits by a temperature T = 3 softens them further: 0.57, 0.24, 0.18. The student is trained to match these (scaled by T²), usually together with the true labels.

f6-t9.title: Speculative decoding: a fast drafter, a careful checker

frames.caption: A big model normally generates one token per slow forward pass.
A small, fast draft model quickly guesses the next 4 tokens: "the cat sat in".
The big model checks all 4 guesses in a single pass (it can score every position at once). It agrees with "the cat sat" and disagrees with "in".

Keep the accepted tokens, and use the big model's own choice ("on") at the first disagreement. 4 tokens for one big-model pass instead of 1. The output is exactly what the big model would have produced on its own; the gain depends on how often the draft is right.

shapes.text: 4 tokens from 1 pass of the big model

f7-t1.title: Variational autoencoders: a tidy latent space you can sample from

frames.caption: An autoencoder squeezes an input (a handwritten digit) through a small code z, then rebuilds it. Training minimises the reconstruction error.
A plain autoencoder's codes (one colour per digit) can scatter anywhere, with gaps between them. Decode a random point in a gap and you get nonsense, so you can't generate new digits.
A VAE's encoder outputs a mean μ and a spread σ, and z is sampled: z = μ + σ·ε with ε ~ N(0, 1). This "reparameterisation trick" lets gradients flow through the sampling.
The ELBO adds a KL term that pulls every code towards a standard bell curve N(0, I). The codes become a tidy, gap-free cloud around the centre.
Now generating is easy: sample any z from N(0, I) and decode it into a new, plausible digit. The price of the noise: VAE samples are often a little blurry.

f7-t2.title: Diffusion: learn to remove noise, then remove it step by step

frames.caption: Training data: 80 points on a spiral (think of each point as one whole image).
The forward process mixes in Gaussian noise: x_t = √ᾱ_t · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε. A little noise first…
…then more. The shape blurs.
At the end it is almost pure noise. Training: pick a random noise level, add noise, and teach a network to predict the noise ε that was added. The loss is plain squared error.
Generating runs the other way. Start from pure noise.
At each step the network predicts the noise, and a small part of it is removed. (Illustration: these frames retrace the noising path backwards.)
Step after step, structure appears.
A new sample from the data distribution. Real models take tens to a thousand of these steps, which is why diffusion is slow; faster samplers and distillation cut that down.

f7-t3.title: Reinforcement learning: values spread back from rewards

frames.caption: A grid world. The agent (yellow) is in a state (a square) and can take an action: move up, down, left or right. Reaching the green square gives reward +1; the red one gives −1.
Nobody tells it the right path. It must learn from rewards, which only arrive at the very end: the credit-assignment problem.
A value function says how much future reward each square leads to. Value iteration, sweep 1: only squares next to the goal know anything yet (discount γ = 0.8).
Sweep 2: value spreads one step further from the goal, shrunk by γ at every step.
After a few sweeps, every square has a value: how good it is to stand there. Farther from the goal means lower value.

The policy (arrows) simply steps towards the highest-value neighbour. Note how it routes around the wall and away from the red pit. Q-learning learns the same kind of values from experience, without knowing the rules in advance.

f7-t4.title: Policy gradients: make good actions more likely, in small steps

frames.caption: A policy network outputs a probability for each action. At first it has no preference.
Play an episode. "right" led to a better-than-average return (positive advantage), so nudge its probability up: ∇ log π(a|s) × advantage.

shapes.text: took "right", return above baseline → more likely

frames.caption: "left" led to a worse-than-average return: its probability goes down.

shapes.text: took "left", return below baseline → less likely

frames.caption: Repeat over many episodes and the policy shifts towards actions that earn more reward. The signal is noisy, which is why a baseline (an average) is subtracted.
PPO looks at the ratio r = π_new(a|s) / π_old(a|s): how much the update changed this action's probability. Here the advantage is positive, so the objective r × A rewards raising it…

…and without limits, a big step could push r far up and wreck the policy. PPO clips: past r = 1 + ε (ε = 0.2) the objective goes flat, so there is no reward for changing the policy further in one update.
So each update stays close to the old policy: small, safe steps that can reuse the same batch of experience several times. This is the algorithm behind classic RLHF for language models.
